 Social Security running out refers to the projected depletion of trust fund reserves, not the program ending — six facts explain what that means for your benefits
 1 / 8 List slides 6 facts about the Social Security trust fund and what depletion means List slides Previous Start over By Colleen Cabili · Updated November 12, 2026 Add QZ to Google Illustration: Quartz
 "Social Security running out" describes a funding gap, not a shutdown. The program pays retirement, disability and survivor benefits largely from payroll taxes that current workers and their employers pay each year. Those taxes do not stop when a reserve account hits zero. What changes is how much of the promised benefit the incoming money can cover.
 Every year, the program's trustees publish a report projecting when the reserves held in its trust funds could be depleted. News coverage often shrinks that projection into a claim that Social Security is going broke or will disappear. The shorthand suggests checks would stop entirely. Under current law, that is not what the projection describes.
 The difference matters to several groups of people. Workers in their 30s and 40s can use it to decide how much to save on their own. Retirees and people near retirement can use it to judge how secure their monthly income is. Financial advisers need it to build realistic plans for clients. Voters need it to weigh the proposals lawmakers put forward to close the gap.
 Reading a depletion headline accurately takes some background. It helps to know how the program collects money and what the trust funds hold. It also helps to know what the law allows the Social Security Administration to do once reserves are gone. A clear reading separates the legal mechanics from the political argument over how to fix the shortfall.
 The projected depletion year and the size of any benefit reduction change with each annual trustees report. Shifts in the economy, birth rates, life expectancy and immigration move the numbers. New legislation can move them too. Readers should check the latest figures directly with the Social Security Administration and the trustees' most recent report.
 The six points that follow explain what the trust funds are and why payroll taxes keep paying benefits after reserves run dry. They cover why depletion would mean a reduction rather than zero benefits. They show how the retirement and disability funds differ. They also explain where the depletion date comes from, why it moves and what Congress can do to change the outcome.
 Social Security trust funds are reserves, not the whole program 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The Social Security trust funds hold reserves that cover the difference when the program's costs exceed its income. Those reserves are not the main source of benefit checks. Most of the money paid to beneficiaries each month comes from taxes on people who are working now.
 That arrangement is known as pay-as-you-go financing. Workers and employers pay in, and the money goes back out to retirees, people with disabilities and the survivors of deceased workers. The trust funds are the accounts that money passes through. Taxes are credited to them, and benefits are paid from them. Each year's income goes mostly toward that year's benefits. The accumulated balance is the reserve, and it works as a cushion rather than as the engine of the system.
 The reserves are not held in cash or in stocks. They are invested in special-issue U.S. Treasury securities, which are not sold to the public. Like other Treasury debt, they are backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government. When the program needs to draw on its reserves, the Treasury redeems those securities. The proceeds then go toward benefits.
 Those securities also earn interest, which is credited to the trust funds as income. Interest is one of three revenue streams, alongside payroll taxes and income taxes on benefits. Any income left after benefits and administrative costs are paid is added to the reserve balance.
 For many years the program collected more than it paid out, and the surplus accumulated. Much of the reserve was built up in the years after Congress passed the Social Security Amendments of 1983. That law changed both taxes and benefits to shore up the program's finances.
 The balance has since reversed. Program costs now exceed total income. The reserves are being drawn down to make up the difference.
 A projected depletion date measures exactly this account. It marks the point at which the reserve balance would reach zero. It does not mark the point at which money stops coming in. The reserves and the program are two separate things, and the size of one does not determine whether the other exists.
 Payroll taxes keep paying benefits after the trust fund is depleted 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Payroll taxes do not stop when the Social Security trust fund reserves run out. Workers and employers keep paying them on every covered paycheck. That money continues to fund most scheduled benefits even after the reserves reach zero.
 The tax behind that revenue is 12.4% of covered wages. Employees pay 6.2%, and their employers pay a matching 6.2%. The employee share is withheld under the Federal Insurance Contributions Act, which is why it often appears as FICA on a pay stub. That same line usually includes a separate Medicare tax, which funds a different program.
 Self-employed workers pay the full 12.4% themselves under the Self-Employment Contributions Act. No employer covers the other half. They can deduct the employer-equivalent half when calculating their adjusted gross income for federal income tax purposes.
 The tax does not apply to every dollar a person earns. It stops at an annual taxable maximum, a wage cap indexed to growth in average wages across the economy. Earnings above the cap are not taxed for Social Security. They also do not count toward a worker's future benefit. The Social Security Administration announces the new cap each fall, alongside the annual cost-of-living adjustment.
 Payroll taxes are the largest source of income for the program, but not the only one. Part of the federal income tax that some beneficiaries pay on their benefits is credited back to the trust funds. Interest earned on the reserves is the third source. That interest ends once the reserves are gone.
 The amount collected depends on the labor market. When more people are working and wages rise, collections grow. When unemployment climbs during a recession, collections weaken.
 Depletion therefore removes one income source, not all of them. Payroll tax revenue still arrives with each pay period, and the income tax on benefits keeps flowing to the program. Together they fall short of the full amount scheduled under current law. They do not drop to zero.
 Social Security would pay reduced benefits, not zero benefits 
 Illustration: Quartz
 If the trust fund reserves are exhausted, current law lets Social Security pay benefits only up to the revenue it still collects. The result would be smaller payments for beneficiaries, not the end of payments.
 That outcome follows from two features of the program's legal design. Social Security has no authority to borrow money to cover a shortfall. It also cannot pay benefits beyond the funds it has available. Once reserves are gone, spending would be capped at whatever income keeps arriving.
 Income would not stop at that point. Payroll taxes on covered wages would keep coming in, along with the income taxes some beneficiaries pay on their benefits. Interest earnings would end, with no reserves left to generate them. The remaining revenue would cover part of scheduled benefits but not all of them.
 The law does not say how a reduction would be carried out. It limits what can be paid but leaves the mechanics unaddressed. No statute specifies whether the Social Security Administration would apply an across-the-board cut to every check or delay payments until enough revenue arrived.
 A reduction would reach people already collecting benefits, not only future retirees. Someone already receiving a monthly check from a depleted trust fund would face the same funding limit as a new claimant. Having started benefits years earlier would not exempt a beneficiary from it.
 The everyday words used to describe this situation can mislead. A household that is broke has nothing left to spend. A company in bankruptcy may stop operating or sell off its assets to pay creditors. Social Security fits neither picture. It would keep collecting revenue and keep sending payments, at a level below what the benefit formula schedules.
 That distinction shapes how a depletion date should be read. The date marks the point when reserves and ongoing income together could no longer pay full scheduled benefits. It does not mark the point when checks stop arriving.
 The OASI and DI trust funds are separate accounts 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Social Security runs on two legally distinct trust funds: the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI) fund and the Disability Insurance (DI) fund. A depletion date in the news usually refers either to OASI alone or to a combined OASDI projection. Those are two different measures.
 The OASI fund pays retirement benefits to retired workers and their eligible spouses and children. It also pays survivor benefits to the widows, widowers and children of workers who have died. It serves the largest group of beneficiaries. That makes it responsible for most of the program's costs.
 The DI fund pays benefits to workers who can no longer work because of a qualifying disability, along with certain members of their families. It has its own income stream and its own balance. Its finances can follow a different path from the retirement fund.
 Federal law sets how payroll tax revenue is divided between the two funds. Neither fund can automatically draw on the other's reserves. Moving money between them takes an act of Congress.
 That is why the combined OASDI figure is a hypothetical measure. It shows when reserves would run out if the two funds were pooled. Current law does not pool them. A headline that cites the combined date is describing a scenario that would need legislation to become real.
 Congress has shifted revenue between the funds before. The Bipartisan Budget Act of 2015 temporarily redirected a share of payroll tax revenue toward DI to keep that fund from being depleted. The change did not add money to Social Security as a whole. It changed which account received the money.
 Medicare's Hospital Insurance (HI) trust fund is a third account that often gets mixed into the discussion. It covers Part A hospital costs and has its own projections and its own depletion date. The same officials serve as trustees for both programs. Because the two programs' projections are often reported together, the HI date is sometimes mistaken for a Social Security figure.
 Supplemental Security Income, a needs-based program that the Social Security Administration also runs, is not paid from either trust fund. It is financed from general Treasury revenue.
 Readers checking a new projection can start with one question: which fund does the date describe? The answer determines which benefits the figure applies to.
 The Social Security trustees report sets the depletion date 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The date when Social Security's reserves are projected to run out comes from an annual report by the program's Boards of Trustees. It is an estimate built on assumptions, and it can move earlier or later from one year to the next.
 The trustees are mostly senior federal officials. The Secretary of the Treasury serves as managing trustee. The Secretary of Labor, the Secretary of Health and Human Services and the Commissioner of Social Security also serve. The law provides for two public trustees as well. The same officials oversee Medicare's trust funds, which are covered in a separate annual report.
 The Social Security report projects the program's income and costs over a 75-year horizon. That window is long enough to follow a worker entering the labor force today through a full career and into retirement. The report measures both when reserves could be depleted and how far income would fall short of costs across that full period.
 The trustees run three sets of assumptions. The intermediate assumptions are their best estimate, and the depletion dates quoted in most news coverage come from that scenario. The low-cost scenario assumes conditions that improve the program's finances. The high-cost scenario assumes conditions that weaken them. The distance between those two outer scenarios shows how sensitive the outlook is to its inputs.
 Those inputs are demographic and economic. Fertility, mortality and immigration shape how many people will be working and paying in, and how many will be collecting benefits. Wage growth and employment determine how much payroll tax revenue comes in. Inflation affects the size of the annual cost-of-living adjustment paid to beneficiaries.
 A change in any one assumption can shift the projected date. A stronger labor market can push it later. A lower birth rate or slower wage growth can pull it closer.
 Legislation also moves the numbers. Any law that changes payroll taxes, benefit rules or the way revenue is allocated alters the projections in the reports that follow it.
 A new report is easier to read with two checks. The first is which set of assumptions produced the headline date. The second is how that date compares with the previous year's projection. Any movement reflects updated data, revised assumptions or new law. The report itself sets out which factors changed its projections from the prior year.
 Congress can close the Social Security funding gap with tax or benefit changes 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Congress can narrow or close the Social Security funding gap by raising revenue, reducing scheduled benefits or combining the two. A projected depletion date reflects current law. Lawmakers have rewritten that law before when reserves ran low.
 The clearest precedent is the Social Security Amendments of 1983. That legislation followed the work of the National Commission on Social Security Reform. The panel is widely known as the Greenspan Commission, after its chairman, Alan Greenspan. The final package changed both the revenue and the benefit sides of the program.
 Two of its provisions still shape Social Security today. The amendments gradually raised the full retirement age from 65 to 67, phasing the increase in over many years. They also made a portion of Social Security benefits subject to federal income tax. The revenue from that tax is credited to the Social Security trust funds.
 The options available now fall into a few broad categories. On the revenue side, Congress could raise the payroll tax rate, which currently totals 12.4% of covered wages. Lawmakers could also raise the annual taxable maximum, which caps the earnings subject to the tax. They could also eliminate the cap entirely. Another route is transferring general revenue from the Treasury into the trust funds.
 On the benefit side, Congress could raise the full retirement age again. It could change the formula used to calculate a person's initial benefit. It could also alter the annual cost-of-living adjustment, which determines how benefits grow after someone starts collecting.
 A separate option concerns how the reserves are managed. The trust funds hold special-issue U.S. Treasury securities. Some proposals would change how those reserves are invested.
 Each lever lands on a different group. Payroll tax increases fall on current workers and employers. A higher or uncapped taxable maximum falls mainly on higher earners. Benefit changes affect retirees, people with disabilities and survivors, depending on how they are designed. Many proposals blend several of these measures rather than relying on one.
 Timing shapes the size of any change. The Social Security trustees have stated in their annual reports that earlier action would allow adjustments to be phased in more gradually. It would also spread the cost across more generations of workers and beneficiaries. Later action leaves fewer years over which to spread the same adjustment.
